name: Pedro Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Riverside Drinks, a family-owned drinks distributor that's been going for three generations. We supply about four hundred pubs, restaurants and corner shops with beer, soft drinks, wine and a bit of spirits. My day is ringing the breweries and the bottlers, watching what's selling, and making sure nobody runs dry before a big football weekend.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what gets you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the people. The brewers, the landlords, old Mr Kowalski who owns the company and still walks the warehouse every Friday. What gets me down is the forms, honestly, the duty paperwork and the new computer system everybody keeps telling me will do it all for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get overblown. At work I'd say it with a smile to the young lads who keep talking about AI. I don't do social media apart from the church group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, relieved about the computers. But AI was never the drinks trade's real problem. Five pubs on my round closed this year, and not one of them closed because of a computer. Riverside's volumes are down, Mr Kowalski is seventy-four, and we've only got about two months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on ringing the brewers first thing and doing the orders the way I always have. I'd push for more cheap soft-drink lines for the corner shops, because they're the part of our trade that's growing while the pubs shrink. At home we'd keep saving our fifty a week and put the autumn trip to Mei's family off until spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the computers, uneasy about the trade. A bit like a farmer who isn't afraid of the new tractor but is watching the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the drinks trade runs on people. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two summers ago a heatwave hit and every distributor ran out of lager. I rang a brewer I've known fifteen years, and he held back forty kegs for us because I'd helped him when his bottling line broke. No computer gets you forty kegs of lager in a heatwave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Mr Kowalski is seventy-four. What happens when he steps back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I don't like thinking about. His son Tomas did a business degree and talks about margins at every Friday meeting. Mr Kowalski won't be walking the warehouse forever, and when Tomas is in charge, I think he'll look hard at who earns what.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because these things always get overblown, and I'd say it with a smile to the young lads at work. I don't do social media apart from the church group.
S0.think: I'm relieved about the computers, but they were never the drinks trade's real problem. Five pubs on my round closed this year, Riverside's volumes are down, Mr Kowalski is seventy-four, and we have only about two months saved.
S0.do: Carries on ringing the brewers first thing and pushes for more cheap soft-drink lines for the growing corner-shop trade. Keeps saving 50 a week and puts the autumn trip to Mei's family off until spring.
S0.feel: Calm about the computers but uneasy about the trade, like a farmer who trusts his tractor but keeps watching the sky.
S0.quote: Five pubs on my round closed this year, and not one of them closed because of a computer.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro's relief about AI sits on top of older worries: pubs closing, falling volumes, thin savings and an owner nearing the end. He trusts Mr Kowalski personally but is clearly uneasy about the son, Tomas, who talks about margins. The forty kegs story shows how much he believes the trade runs on favours.

steps.text: Keep ringing the brewers first thing each morning
Push for cheap soft-drink lines for the growing corner-shop trade
Keep saving 50 a week towards the thin cushion
Put off the autumn trip to Mei's family until spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Riverside is a family firm and they look after their people, and that's the truth so far. At work I'd say I'll do whatever's needed. At church I'd say a prayer for the ones who lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried, because buying is what I do and the card says buying goes to the computers. If the other distributors use AI to buy cheaper and faster, Riverside has to do the same or lose the pubs. Old Mr Kowalski has kept people on through two recessions, but a kind owner can't keep a buyer the computer has replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Mr Kowalski and ask him straight what his plans are for the buying side, which I've never done in twelve years. If they put me on training, I'd go, though I'd find it hard, but I wouldn't pay for a course myself until I see what Riverside does. At home I'd cut the takeaway night and the sports channel and put another twenty-five a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it and not tell Mei how much it's on my mind, though she'd know anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust Mr Kowalski. What if his son takes over in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Kowalski's son Tomas takes over the company, I'd be less sure, and I'd start looking. Tomas would keep someone on the phones, maybe, but at less money. I'd ask about the delivery side before I'd let them hand me an envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about two months saved, what goes first if money gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The takeaway night and the sports channel go first, then the trip to Mei's family. I wouldn't touch the children's church camp. I'd ask my brother about weekend shifts at his restaurant before I'd ask anyone for money.

S1.say: I'd say Riverside is a family firm that looks after its people, which is true so far, and that I'll do whatever's needed. At church I'd pray for the ones who lose out.
S1.think: Buying is what I do, and the computers will take buying. If rivals buy cheaper with AI, Riverside must follow, and even a kind owner like Mr Kowalski can't keep a buyer the computer has replaced.
S1.do: Asks Mr Kowalski outright, for the first time in twelve years, what he plans for the buying side, and goes to any training Riverside offers but won't pay for a course himself yet. Cuts the takeaway night and the sports channel and saves another 25 a week, with his brother's restaurant shifts as a fallback.
S1.feel: Anxious. He prays about it and hides from Mei how much it's on his mind, though she'd know.
S1.quote: Old Mr Kowalski has kept people on through two recessions, but a kind owner can't keep a buyer the computer has replaced.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro's trust in a loyal owner no longer feels like protection once buying itself is on the card; he expects his role to shrink or move to lower pay. For a man who waits to be pushed, asking Mr Kowalski straight out is a big step. Family and his brother come before any outside help.

steps.text: Wait for Riverside's plan before paying for any course himself
Cut the takeaway night and the sports channel
Save an extra 25 a week on top of the usual 50
Ask his brother about restaurant shifts if money gets tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let this rush in with nobody ready. I'd say people need to stand on their own feet, but you can't stand on your feet when the floor's pulled away overnight. At church we'd talk about who needs help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even Mr Kowalski couldn't keep me on. If his competitors use AI to buy cheaper and faster, Riverside either does the same or goes under. My job, the phoning and ordering, is exactly the sort of thinking work that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no trip, no takeaways, cancel the sports channel. I'd ask Mr Kowalski for a job on the delivery side, driving the dray lorry, because I know every pub and robots aren't coming for that until about 2031. And I'd talk to my brother, who runs a restaurant, about shifts if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and not sleeping much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd drive the dray lorry. How would that feel after years as a buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humbling, I won't pretend otherwise. My father drove a bread van for thirty years and raised four kids on it, so honest work doesn't embarrass me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if it were offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'd go to family and the church first, that's how we've always done it. But with a mortgage and two kids, if it came to that, I'd swallow my pride.

S2.say: I'd say it's madness to let this rush in with nobody ready, because you can't stand on your own feet when the floor is pulled away overnight. At church we'd talk about who needs help.
S2.think: Even the owner couldn't keep me on, because competitors using AI would force Riverside to do the same or go under. Phoning and ordering is exactly the thinking work that goes first.
S2.do: Cancels the trip, takeaways and sports channel straight away. Asks Mr Kowalski for a dray lorry driving job until robots arrive around 2031, and asks his brother about restaurant shifts.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying a lot and sleeping little.
S2.quote: My father drove a bread van for thirty years and raised four kids on it, so honest work doesn't embarrass me.
S2.fieldNote: Pedro's free-market view leads him to see that loyalty can't survive competitors using AI. He reaches for hands-on work, family and church before any government help. The story of his father's bread van gives him pride in stepping down.

steps.text: Cancel the trip, takeaways and the sports channel
Ask Mr Kowalski for a job driving the dray lorry
Ask his brother about shifts at the restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and a man should use it to provide for his family. At work I'd say we need a plan for the old hands, not just the young ones. At church I'd say we should help each other get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still find it hard to act before I see it. I'd be 48 in 2031. I think I'd keep my job until near the end and then move to the lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more aside, maybe another thirty a week, to get from about two months of savings to four. I'd keep buying the old way while Riverside lets me. I'd probably get my heavy goods licence around 2029, so the driving job is ready when the buying goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than the fast one. I'd feel I had a bit of a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until 2029 for the licence, rather than now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Simple. I don't want to spend money on a lorry licence for something that might never happen. If I see Riverside bringing the system in, then I'll do it. That's how I am, careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace is ten, she doesn't need to carry this. I'd tell her Dad's job might change and that's fine, God provides. Mei would be the one who worries out loud.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning and a man should use it to provide for his family. At work I'd ask for a plan for the old hands, and at church I'd urge people to help each other.
S3.think: I'd still find it hard to act before I see it. I'd keep my job until near the end in 2031 and then move to the lorries.
S3.do: Saves another thirty a week to grow savings from about two months to four. Keeps buying the old way and plans to get a heavy goods licence around 2029 for a driving job when buying goes.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, with a sense of having a path.
S3.quote: I don't want to spend money on a lorry licence for something that might never happen.
S3.fieldNote: Pedro uses the extra time mainly to delay, saving more but waiting to see before spending on a licence. His plan relies on the robot lag protecting driving work. He shields his young daughter and leans on faith for reassurance.

steps.text: Save another thirty a week towards four months of savings
Get a heavy goods licence around 2029 if Riverside brings in AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and nobody should panic. A sensible man saves, works hard and looks after his family, whatever happens. That's what I'd say at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 when it arrives. If I keep my head down, the mortgage is mostly paid by then, and I'd have a few years of driving before the robots in 2039. I'd be uneasy, but I don't think it would change much for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and keep saving the extra each week. I'd overpay the mortgage when the summer trade is good. I'd keep away from the new systems as long as Riverside lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like knowing winter's coming but it's still summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep away from the new systems. Isn't that a risk over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Mei says so too. But I'm not good with screens, and by the time I've learned one, they change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to take from this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family and faith don't get automated, and the people around your table are still there when jobs come and go. I'd want Daniel and Grace to know that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and nobody should panic: a sensible man saves, works hard and looks after his family. I'd say that at work and at church.
S4.think: I'd be 53, with the mortgage mostly paid and a few years of driving before robots in 2039. I'd be uneasy but expect little to change for a long while.
S4.do: Carries on as normal and keeps saving the extra each week. Overpays the mortgage when summer trade is good and avoids the new systems as long as Riverside allows.
S4.feel: Uneasy, like knowing winter is coming while it's still summer.
S4.quote: Family and faith don't get automated, and the people around your table are still there when jobs come and go.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Pedro settles back into his habits and openly admits avoiding the new systems is a risk. His deepest reassurance comes from family and faith, not work. The robot lag fits neatly into his plan to move into driving late in his career.

steps.text: Keep buying the old way and avoid the new systems
Overpay the mortgage when the summer trade is good

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years doesn't give a careful man time to be careful. What would help is employers being made to give long notice and offer the hands-on jobs to their own people first, before hiring outside. And cheap training for a lorry licence, because that costs money we don't have spare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pubs. When a landlord's cellar runs dry on a Saturday night, he rings a person he trusts, not a program. A landlord's trust is built over years, and I don't think it moves over to a machine that easily.

headlineQuote: When a landlord's cellar runs dry on a Saturday night, he rings a person he trusts, not a program.
portrait: Pedro Chen, 43, buys beer, wine and soft drinks for Riverside Drinks, a three-generation family distributor. He has never used AI and believes the drinks trade runs on handshakes and favours, like the forty kegs a brewer saved him in a heatwave. Even if AI stalls he is uneasy, with pubs closing, about two months saved and an owner nearing seventy-five, and under steady change he is anxious, sure that even a loyal owner can't keep a buyer the computer has replaced. AGI by 2028 alarms him, and in every AGI picture he plans to step down to driving the dray lorry, leaning on family and church before government. With more time he mostly waits, saving a little more and avoiding the new systems.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years doesn't give a careful man time to be careful.
whatWouldHelp: Long notice from employers, hands-on jobs offered to their own staff first, and cheap training for a lorry licence.
